talks.title: More Than Data: Making Knowledge Graphs Work Together for Actionable Insights
talks.speaker: Prof. Dr. Ricardo Usbeck
talks.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have driven remarkable progress in natural language processing, their application in high-stakes, dynamic environments remains constrained by limited factual grounding, interpretability, and user trust. To address these fundamental challenges, our research group (https://www.leuphana.de/aix) investigates the neuro-symbolic integration of state-of-the-art language models with a multitude of dynamic knowledge graphs. By anchoring generative architectures in structured, continuously updated real-world facts, we enable AI systems to predict supply chain reliability or the trajectories of natural disasters. This keynote will highlight our recent contributions to the deployment of domain-specific, autonomous AI agents for crisis management and supply chain resilience. Drawing on insights from the COYPU, PROVIDER, and RescueMate projects - where robust, real-time event extraction from heterogeneous global data streams is critical - this talk will show how only a collection of integrated Knowledge Graphs can provide the verifiable ground truth necessary to deploy autonomous AI in environments where failure is not an option.

Second International Workshop on Users and Knowledge Graphs (UKG)

Knowledge graphs (KGs) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for representing and managing complex information, underpinning numerous applications from search engines to personalized recommendations. However, the true potential of KGs can only be realized if users effectively utilize them. This workshop focuses on the critical intersection of users and KGs. It explores how individuals interact with KGs, their challenges, and the innovative solutions that can bridge the gap between KG technology and user needs. We aim to foster discussions that improve the usability, accessibility, assessment, and adoption of KGs in real-world scenarios. We invite submissions presenting user studies, case studies, novel applications of KGs designed with user-centricity and explainability in mind, and research exploring the cognitive and interactional aspects of KG use. This workshop aims to foster a vibrant discussion on the future of user-centred KG design and development. It will feature paper presentations, interactive discussions, demos, and a panel session to encourage engagement between researchers and practitioners.

talks.title: From Paraphrase to Provenance: Building a Verbatim Claim-Spine from Spoken-Word Archives
talks.speaker: Chad Nantais, Syntopic
talks.abstract:
Most pipelines that turn unstructured text or audio into a knowledge graph quietly introduce a provenance gap. A language model is asked to extract "the claims," and it returns fluent paraphrases that no speaker ever actually said, often stamped with timestamps the model guessed rather than measured. The resulting graph reads well and cites nothing verifiable. This talk is a lessons-learned account of discovering that failure mode in a production pipeline and rearchitecting the extraction around a strict provenance contract.

The setting is Syntopic, a boutique service that transforms finished podcast back-catalogs into research-grade companion sites with synced transcripts, entity pages, and full-text search over a structured claim graph. Our worked example is an 81-episode philosophy archive (roughly 170 hours of audio) rendered into a navigable knowledge graph of claims, concepts, people, and works. Midway through the build we found our extraction was storing synthesized claim prose with LLM-estimated timestamps rather than verbatim spans anchored to deterministic, word-level speech-to-text output. That violated the core promise of the product, so we paused and separated every claim into a normalized headline plus one or more verbatim grounding spans, each carrying a derived timestamp from word-level Whisper output and an epistemic status tag (asserted, hedged, contested, or reported).

The talk covers the schema decisions this forced (stable entity IDs and canonical names kept separate from surface mentions, so the graph can survive re-processing and multi-client federation without migration), the human-in-the-loop correction log we capture as a compounding training asset, and the practical entity-resolution ceiling we hit as archives grow past a couple hundred episodes. The aim is to share concrete, reproducible tactics for anyone extracting grounded, citable claims from speech, where the difference between "sounds right" and "provably said" is the whole point.

A live companion site for a completed 81-episode archive will be available at presentation time.

talks.title: The Universal CPQ Interface: Exploring Product Configuration Models via MCP and Knowledge Graphs
talks.speaker: Marcel Fröhlich, eccenca GmbH
talks.abstract:
Product configuration models in CPQ systems are typically proprietary and opaque, creating vendor lock-in and limiting flexibility. This talk presents a solution using knowledge graphs and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to represent these models in a vendor-neutral, standardized format. By exposing configuration logic as a knowledge graph, organizations can explore models through MCP tools and translate them into any CPQ system’s language—without being tied to a specific vendor’s proprietary format.

We discuss how this general representation serves as a universal interface for product configuration knowledge, breaking vendor dependencies while maintaining full access to the underlying logic. The talk covers the technical foundation, practical benefits for model exploration and migration, and its contribution to interoperable knowledge management in enterprise environments.

talks.title: Transforming a Database into a Conversational Knowledge Graph: Tales from the ScaleTrust Project
talks.speaker: Felix Brei, Institute for Applied Informatics (InfAI)
talks.abstract:
How can a traditional data marketplace evolve into a conversational Knowledge Graph that enables users to discover data without having to understand complex query languages or graph structures? This talk presents the evolution of the ScaleTrust project, following the transformation of a relational database into a Knowledge Graph and, ultimately, into a conversational interface powered by an LLM agent.

Starting from a data marketplace backed by a relational database, the project introduced an RDF-based Knowledge Graph to enable users to explore datasets through their relationships, properties, keywords, categories, and authors. The talk describes the resulting RDF pipeline, including JSON-to-RDF mapping with YARRRML, SHACL validation, storage and querying with Apache Jena/Fuseki, and versioning with QuitStore. While this graph-based approach enabled richer exploration, it still required users to find an initial entry point and interact with a rather technical interface.

The next step was therefore to introduce an LLM agent capable of conducting the initial search and interacting with the Knowledge Graph through dedicated tools such as keyword search and SPARQL queries. Based on a ReAct architecture, the agent combines the ScaleTrust Knowledge Graph with external knowledge sources, evaluates results through sub-agents, and can even support users in submitting requests when no suitable dataset is found.

The talk shares the technical approach, lessons learned, and practical experiences from implementing this transformation within roughly one year, demonstrating how Semantic Web technologies and LLMs can complement each other to make Knowledge Graph-based data discovery more accessible.

talks.title: Semantica: A Context and Accountability Layer for Knowledge Graph-Powered AI System (online)
talks.speaker: Mohammad Kaif, Semantica
talks.abstract:
Knowledge Graphs have become an essential component of modern AI systems, yet most LLM-based applications still rely on vector stores and short-term memory mechanisms that provide limited explainability, provenance, and accountability. As AI systems move into production, particularly in regulated domains, there is a growing need for systems that can answer not only what was generated, but also why a decision was made and where the underlying evidence originated.

In this talk, we present Semantica, an open-source framework that introduces Context Graphs as a persistent intelligence layer for AI systems. Semantica combines knowledge graph construction, provenance tracking, deterministic reasoning, ontology management, and temporal intelligence in a single platform. The framework supports the complete lifecycle of knowledge graphs, from multi-source ingestion and information extraction to entity resolution, reasoning, governance, and interactive exploration.

We will demonstrate how Context Graphs extend traditional Knowledge Graphs by treating decisions, evidence, and provenance as first-class graph entities, enabling explainable AI, auditable decision histories, and richer GraphRAG workflows. We also discuss practical applications in regulatory intelligence, compliance, and enterprise AI systems, and explore opportunities for integrating provenance-aware and reasoning-centric capabilities into the broader DBpedia ecosystem.

Scientific data is often sparse, noisy, and domain-specific, requiring models to understand and adhere to rigorous scientific principles and constraints. Issues such as model interpretability, reproducibility, and ethical use are particularly critical in scientific applications, where errors or biases can have far-reaching consequences.

title: Bridging Law and AI: Semantic Precision without Compromising Trust
label: Tutorial
chair: Ingrid Thurlings and Janneke van der Zwaan
description:
Bridging Law and AI: Semantic Precision without Compromising Trust

Translating legislation into digital implementations is a labor-intensive process. It requires analyzing large volumes of legal text with a level of accuracy and reliability that typically demands a multidisciplinary team of both legal and IT experts. Currently, this work is largely done by hand, translating legislation into structured knowledge, creating legal knowledge graphs based on legal ontologies, where legal norms are translated into logical if-then rules. Although (generative) AI has been explored for interpreting legislation, it has so far not led to a major breakthrough. In practice, existing solutions have proven to be insufficiently reliable. As legal analysis comprises of many steps, our research investigates which steps of legal analysis are most likely to be accelerated or (partially) automated using AI, large language models and machine learning, without compromising accuracy and reliability. The initial focus is on identifying accurate candidate definitions for key legal concepts, including their precise knowledge references, given strict definition guidelines. Secondly, we build on our previous work (“A New Approach to Taxonomy Creation”) to generate candidate taxonomies with definitions written according to the same guidelines. In this tutorial we will share our results and give a live demo of what is currently possible. We look forward to active participation, discussing the most promising way forward and the challenges that arising when combining semantic and AI technology in the domain of legal analysis.

talks.title: Classifying Classes in Wikidata
talks.speaker: Ege Atacan Doğan, JMU Würzburg
talks.abstract:
In Wikidata there are many classes but many of them do not have direct instances. For example, builder is a class in Wikidata, yet everyone who is a builder is typed only as human and has occupation builder.  This is a representational choice in Wikidata.  Wikidata has many instances of human, which are also instances of organism, but no human is directly marked as an instance of organism.  There is no fundamental reason to not allow direct instances of organization, but in Wikidata human is the "appropriate" class for humans. The question then becomes: how can these choices be maintained at the scale of Wikidata, particularly with the many editors of Wikidata.

One distinction that helps is sortality. Human, tree, and astronomical object type are sortal concepts. These classes individuate and supply identity criteria. Jazz, red, and happiness are not sortal. There are no things that are instances of them.  Wikidata offers no built-in way to mark this difference, but the distribution of direct instance assertions provides empirical signal.

Within sortal classes, a second distinction matters: not every sortal is the "right" sortal for typing. Organism is too generic to be informative, male builder is too specific and, perhaps more importantly, non-rigid. The Wikidata community has converged on a preferred level of granularity, and we can see this choice in the density of direct instance assertions.

We propose a six-way categorisation of entities with respect to direct instance usage: individuals, appropriate classes, too-vague classes, too-specific classes, appropriate classes with no typed instances, and non-sortal classes that stand outside this dynamic entirely. We use intensional assumptions that are supported by what the classes "mean" to distinguish these categories. The result can be used to detect class-ordering problems and formalise the "appropriate class" modeling pattern.

talks.title: An Explainable Hybrid GraphRAG Framework for Diabetes Risk Stratification (online)
talks.speaker: Herman Kandolo, Vietnam National University & La Rochelle Université
talks.abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly improved the usability of clinical decision support systems, but they still suffer from high context consumption and limited explainability when reasoning over medical data. We present an explainable Hybrid GraphRAG framework that shifts statistical reasoning from the LLM to a deterministic knowledge graph, allowing the language model to focus exclusively on generating clinician-friendly explanations. The framework combines unsupervised learning, supervised classification, Neo4j-based knowledge graphs, and LLM-based natural language generation into a unified decision-support pipeline.

The system builds epidemiological knowledge from the BRFSS 2015 dataset through K-Means clustering and stores the resulting profiles in a Neo4j knowledge graph. During online inference, a new patient is assigned to the most appropriate epidemiological profile using a K-NN classifier. The corresponding statistical evidence is retrieved through Cypher queries and provided to the LLM as a compact and fully auditable context for explanation generation. Experimental results demonstrate a 97.31% reduction in LLM context size compared with a vector-based RAG baseline while eliminating numerical hallucinations in our evaluation and providing fully traceable decision evidence. The presentation will demonstrate the complete workflow of the prototype and discuss how deterministic knowledge graphs can improve transparency and trust in GraphRAG-based clinical decision support systems.

talks.title: DBpedia KG Catalog
talks.speaker: Milan Dojchinovski, InfAI/DBpedia Association, TIB, CTU Prague
talks.abstract:
The Knowledge Graph ecosystem is rapidly growing, but discovering, understanding, and reusing Knowledge Graphs remains challenging: Where are relevant Knowledge Graphs? What do they contain? Which versions are available, and where can the data be accessed?

This talk introduces the DBpedia Knowledge Graph Catalog, an initiative for discovering, describing, and reusing Knowledge Graphs. While the Linked Open Data Cloud focuses on datasets, links, and the broader ecosystem, the KG Catalog takes a complementary perspective centred on Knowledge Graphs, their metadata, releases, and artifacts. Versioning, access, and machine-readable metadata are treated as first-class elements, enabling not only discovery but also operational reuse.

The talk presents the motivation and concepts behind the KG Catalog, demonstrates how Knowledge Graphs can be described and accessed through the catalog, and provides a live demonstration using real-world examples. Finally, it introduces the broader vision of building a comprehensive Knowledge Graph landscape and invites the community to contribute by cataloging Knowledge Graphs, curating metadata, and building services on top of the catalog.

Please join the KG Catalog Initiative: https://kg-catalog.dbpedia.org.

title: From SOPs to Agent-Ready Semantic Layers: Business Rules, Business Objects, and Data Grounding for Enterprise AI
label: Tutorial
description:
From SOPs to Agent-Ready Semantic Layers: Business Rules, Business Objects, and Data Grounding for Enterprise AI

Enterprises have built extensive data infrastructure, but their data products, operational guidance, and AI agents often lack a shared business context. Concepts such as Customer, Account, or Policy are defined differently across systems. SOPs and policy documents refer to these concepts without explicit connections to the underlying data, while agents are developed with their own tools and hand-wired grounding. Connecting these assets through shared business meaning creates a foundation for reuse, traceability, and governed enterprise AI. This tutorial introduces the Enterprise Semantic Layer as a machine-readable abstraction spanning physical assets such as schemas, APIs, and services; logical mappings; and business definitions, processes, capabilities, and ownership. Its central argument is that Business Object ontologies provide a common point of connection for data, operational guidance, and agents. Data product schemas are represented in RDF and mapped to these ontologies, establishing how business concepts are represented across heterogeneous sources and where their data can be found. SOPs, policy documents, and individual rules are represented as entities in the same graph and linked to the Business Objects they reference. A rule containing a condition about a customer can therefore connect to a shared definition of Customer and, through the mappings, to the data products supplying the relevant information. The rule retains its authored wording while gaining a traceable path to the data needed to apply it. Cataloguing agents, the rules they handle, and the tools they use brings execution into this shared context. Recording what tools read, what they write, and which systems they act against makes dependencies visible across operational guidance, agents, and data. Links to business processes, capabilities, and functions extend this traceability to the enterprise activities they support. A live demonstration will show a Customer Business Object ontology mapped across four non-semantic data products, enabling unified discovery and federated queries across sources with no common schema. The tutorial will also explain how the same Business Objects connect procedural guidance and agents to this data foundation, and how open semantic standards keep these connections portable across systems and vendors. The session is intended for practitioners and researchers working on knowledge graphs, semantic governance, enterprise AI, ontology engineering, and multi-agent systems. Learning objectives By the end of the session, participants will understand how to: - Construct an Enterprise Semantic Layer across physical, logical, and business levels. - Represent data product schemas in RDF and map them to shared Business Object ontologies. - Enable semantic discovery and federated queries across heterogeneous data products. - Connect SOPs, policy documents, and individually referenceable rules to Business Objects while preserving their authored text. - Trace business concepts referenced in rules to the data products supplying the relevant information. - Catalogue agents, the rules they handle, and their tools, including inputs, outputs, and target systems. - Trace dependencies across rules, agents, data sources, and business capabilities to support governance and change impact analysis.

DBpedia 2026: Creating Opportunities for the DBpedia Community

What could a more community-driven future for DBpedia look like? This session invites DBpedia contributors, chapter leads, organisations and community members to discuss how we can work together to address long-standing challenges and further develop DBpedia.

The discussion will explore a possible community model built around four key elements: a shared Knowledge Graph Lifecycle System (KGLS) and interoperable services; DBpedia Community Projects such as language, thematic and regional initiatives; shared infrastructure and operations; and new roles and opportunities for community members and organisations to contribute, lead projects and support the DBpedia ecosystem.

The session is intended as an open discussion to gather perspectives, ideas and concrete opportunities for collaboration and to jointly shape the future of the DBpedia community.

description:
Developers Workshop

Semantic Web and Knowledge Graph technologies have undoubtedly had a tremendous impact on today’s world. While academia and industry are both highly active in this field, there is often a disconnect between these two worlds. As such, there is a need to bring these two worlds closer together. The goal of this workshop is to provide a bridge between academia and industry in the form of a developers workshop. In this workshop, we invite developers of both worlds to present and discuss their software. description:

talks.title: KGXL-Query: Extending SPARQL with Semantic Search and LLM functionality for Question Answering over Heterogeneous Data 🎖️
talks.speaker: Tilahun Abedissa Taffa, Patrick Westphal, Debayan Banerjee and Ricardo Usbeck
talks.abstract: In this paper, we introduce KGXL-Query, a new SPARQL functionality extension that embeds LLMs (Large Language Models) and semantic search directly into SPARQL, enabling hybrid inference where symbolic and non-symbolic methods coexist within a single, executable, and explainable framework. The quest to answer complex questions, those requiring both structured facts and contextual evidence from unstructured data, has shown a gap in knowledge systems: the incompatibility between symbolic and semantic inference. Knowledge Graphs (KGs) support formal, logically grounded querying via structured languages such as SPARQL. Conversely, LLMs and semantic text search offer vast coverage of real-world knowledge via vector-based similarity metrics. However, beyond using KGs for refining text or LLM results, and complementing missing information in KGs via LLMs or text search, there is less emphasis on accessing LLMs \& semantic search functionality through SPARQL. Moreover, existing Question Answering (QA) methods on heterogeneous data sources use RAG, data unification, and decompose-and-aggregate methods. The unifying approaches suffer from irreversible information loss; decomposition-driven methods are prone to cascading errors; and RAG methods lack explainability and are limited to shallow textual integration. Therefore, KGXL-Query paves the way by transforming the question to leverage the model rather than altering the data to fit it.

talks.title: Navigating Schema Drift: Orchestrating Agents and Schema Discovery for Robust, Domain-specific Knowledge Graph Question Answering
talks.speaker: Anton Diettrich, Dirk Friedenberger and Andreas Both
talks.abstract: Knowledge Graph Question Answering (KGQA) over Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly translates natural-language questions into SPARQL, yet most systems are statically optimized for a single benchmark and degrade abruptly under cross-domain transfer or schema evolution—a recurring obstacle for industrial Knowledge Graphs whose schemas continuously evolve.  We present a KG-agnostic Text2SPARQL architecture that operates without task-specific fine-tuning. A meta-controller orchestrates a ReAct agent and an execution-validated, schema-guided fallback pipeline; both paths are grounded by a runtime FAISS-indexed Schema-Discovery service that absorbs structural change without offline retraining. The system is evaluated across four heterogeneous KGs: the open-domain DBpedia, a structurally complex Corporate dataset, and two versions of a proprietary railway metadata KG (TrackVideo, German: Streckenvideo), whose v1→v2 transition exhibits a Mapping Ratio of 0.255 and a normalized graph edit distance of 0.750, representing radical schema refactoring.  The hybrid architecture attains a mean F1 of 47.6% with the lowest cross-domain standard deviation (2.33) among compared state-of-the-art systems and preserves performance between TrackVideo v1 (48.0%) and v2 (48.6%) despite the drift. A multi-model Quorum extension over heterogeneous LLM families further increases reliability, with absolute F1 gains of up to +7.0%. The findings support the HARP paradigm—hybrid agentic retrieval with execution-validated routing—for portable, schema-drift-resilient KGQA in production-grade settings.

talks.title: GRMP: An open-source platform for automatic monitoring of linked data resources on the web
talks.speaker: Stijn Denis, Marc Portier, Cedric Decruw and Stijn Deknudt
talks.abstract: When publishing linked data-related resources through the web, it is strongly advised to actively monitor them and ensure they remain accessible, up-to-date and continue to provide data in the intended manner. Public registries and dashboards do exist, but they require active maintenance themselves lest they become outdated and provide incorrect information regarding the status of these resources.  In order to support the management of their own LDES-servers and SPARQL endpoints and monitor the status of external web resources they consume, the scientific institute VLIZ (Vlaams Instituut voor de Zee – Flanders Marine Institute) developed GRMP (Graph Resources Monitoring Platform) in cooperation with Flemish IT and Software company Sirus. GRMP is an open-source and highly modular platform which allows for the automatic monitoring of linked data resources and web resources in general.  GRMP is container-based and primarily consists of an orchestrator which manages and directs test suite containers based on configurations defined in one or more YAML-files. Due to its modular nature, users can rapidly develop new test suites in any desired programming language provided that they have been containerized and adhere to a few guidelines allowing for proper communication with the orchestrator.  Additionally, the environment on top of which the system runs can be freely chosen, ranging from local deployments to integration with automation workflows like GitHub Actions. When running within GitHub Actions, additional features are available such as automatic issue creation resulting from failed tests.  This talk by Stijn Denis from Sirus will provide an overview and demonstration of the current VLIZ GRMP implementation, highlighting how it can be rapidly customized and/or expanded upon for use by any organization to automatically run regularly scheduled test suites and monitor resources on the web.

talks.title: Designing Enterprise Semantics: From Models to Meaningful AI [SP]
talks.speaker: Sachin Khungar (GraphWise)
talks.abstract: This talk explores the critical shift from viewing semantics as a purely technical exercise to understanding it as the foundation of shared meaning within an enterprise. By examining architectural patterns, common anti-patterns, and essential governance practices, the session outlines the Enterprise Semantic Design Pyramid and explains why successful initiatives must prioritize business strategy over technology. Attendees will gain a framework for navigating semantic challenges through established design principles and a maturity model — ultimately learning how to transform semantics from a technical feature into a core business capability that enables truly meaningful and autonomous AI.

talks.title: Research wanted [SP]
talks.speaker: Aad Versteden (redpencil.io)
talks.abstract: The web was built on open standards — and so should your software. At redpencil, we build modular, open source applications grounded in W3C standards like RDF, SPARQL, LDES and RDFa. These are not just technical choices: they are architectural decisions that guarantee interoperability, longevity and freedom from vendor lock-in.We bridge the gap between research-grade technology and real-world business problems. Our applications are built to be user-friendly — the semantic complexity stays under the hood, invisible to end users, while delivering data that is meaningful, traceable and reusable by design. We have proven this in production — from local government decision platforms and region-wide data registrations to the central decision-making infrastructure of the Flemish Government.This talk shows how open standards, modular architecture and open source combine into a sovereign, scalable alternative to the monolithic platforms that dominate today's digital landscape — and why that matters more than ever in a world where technological independence has become a strategic necessity.

talks.title: Declaratively Populating Wikibases with WBML
talks.speaker: Élena Liu, Jakub Duchateau and Christophe Debruyne
talks.abstract: Purpose: This paper addresses the lack of a general declarative approach for generating Wikibase content from heterogeneous data sources. Existing declarative mapping approaches mainly target RDF, while Wikibase-oriented solutions are often limited in scope or procedural in nature. We therefore propose WBML, a declarative mapping language tailored to the Wikibase statement model.  Methodology: WBML was designed by reusing selected RML concepts for logical sources and iterations, while introducing Wikibase-specific constructs. We implemented a Python prototype that translates WBML into intermediate RML and RDF representations, executes them with Morph-KGC, and ingests the results into Wikibase.  Findings: The study shows that declaratively generating Wikibase statements from heterogeneous sources is feasible. We also reported on a demonstration using complex JSON and a simpler, real-world use case for our institution, using CSV files. WBML supports the generation of entities, fingerprints, statements, qualifiers, references, and ranks.  Value: This work provides a basis for declarative construction of Wikibase knowledge graphs from heterogeneous sources. It demonstrates how established ideas from the RDF mapping community can be adapted to other types of knowledge graphs. Future work includes supporting newer RML features not yet supported by reused components and managing updates.

talks.title: From Spreadsheets to Shared Understanding: Navigating Water Catchment Data with a Composable Linked Data Architecture
talks.speaker: Andrew Fergusson and Chris Jarvis
talks.abstract: Environmental regulators hold the data that citizens, consultants, planners, and engineers need to understand their local water catchments — discharge permits, monitoring records, land-use classifications, and water quality measurements. Yet broad technical and domain expertise is currently required to identify and use the right datasets, creating a significant FAIR data gap that limits the social, economic, and environmental value that this data could otherwise deliver. The Environment Agency (EA) and Telespazio have addressed this through a composable Linked Data architecture built on the DEFRA Data Services Platform Application Profile — a federation standard aligned to W3C SKOS, DCAT, SOSA/SSN, OWL, and OGC GeoSPARQL. The platform enables domain teams to publish standards-compliant Linked Data APIs from existing data sources, without requiring schema harmonisation or bespoke integration code. Domain systems retain their own vocabularies and express — once — how their terms relate to the shared profile; the federated layer handles the rest. The Water Catchment Demonstrator presents a live user journey grounded in EA's open data. Starting from any location in the United Kingdom, the system identifies the relevant river catchment and traverses the federated data layer to surface discharge permits, compliance monitoring returns, water quality observations, and land-use classifications — without the user needing to know where any dataset lives or how to interpret its observational data. The demonstrator evaluates the Application Profile and technical approaches as a practical federation standard for DEFRA and EA's open data, and provides evidence that composable Linked Data architecture can meaningfully reduce the expertise barrier to accessing and using complex regulatory datasets.

talks.title: A Knowledge-Graph for Utrecht’s Asset Management
talks.speaker: Hans Schevers and Jakko Heinen
talks.abstract: This presentation will present the architecture and operational experience of the Municipality of Utrecht's Single Source of Truth system, called the ObjectRegistration for public asset management. This is a system built by BIM-Connected using their lowcode Linked Data system Wistor. In this case Wistor uses the T-Box (Object Type Library) IMBOR from the dutch standardisation organisation CROW and converted all asset data into Linked Data complying to the IMBOR t-box. The base of the system is a triplestore containing the IMBOR dataset, all asset data information and changelogs. Effectively a knoweldge graph of the public assets of the municipality of Utrecht in the Netherlands. The Utrecht Object Registration clearly demonstrates that a knowledge-graph approach, combining a standardised ontology, linked data infrastructure, live synchronisation, and SHACL-driven governance, is a viable and practically operational foundation for smart city asset management.

talks.title: Knowledge-driven Data Exchange and Validation Framework for Networked Smart Buildings
talks.speaker: Xander Wilcke, Barry Nouwt, Sophie Lathouwers and Ronald Siebes
talks.abstract: Building Automation and Management Systems offer centralized control and monitoring by integrating smart devices into the environment. Together, these provide building owners and stakeholders with data about energy consumption and other relevant characteristics which can, among others, be used for decision making and the automation of actions. However, due to the proliferation of different protocols and ecosystems, it often remains challenging to seamlessly aggregate and analyse the data streams provided by the connected devices. To overcome these problems, we introduce a knowledge-driven data exchange and validation framework, built upon Semantic Web technologies, that a) facilitates the transparent flow of graph data between smart devices, b) validates these data and generates reports on detected anomalous behaviour in real-time, and c) aggregates and displays the data and any derived insight on dashboards and other interactive web-accessible interfaces. Our framework consists of two core components: the Knowledge Engine, which acts as an information broker and translation layer between device-specific languages and RDF, and the Knowledge Validator, which continuously monitors these RDF streams and reports on deviations from nominal behaviour. We evaluate our framework via requirement-based testing and demonstrate its functionality in a real-world case study in the smart buildings domain, showing that it can facilitate seamless communication between devices of different make and model and that it can help building owners recognize abnormal device behaviour.

talks.title: Smart Buildings, Smart Future: Semantic Data Integration for Smart Buildings including a Federated Data Model
talks.speaker: Apostolos Barekas, Pieter Pauwels and Stefan Hoekstra
talks.abstract: Our buildings are getting more and more data-driven, thus providing the potential of making them smarter and ‘more intelligent’. However, 90% of available IoT and sensor data in building systems currently tends to go to waste, and remains unused. This operational data loss is caused by data fragmentation, the use of isolated and often proprietary closed systems, and the absence of standardized data exchange protocols, obstacles that consistently prevent building owners from deploying affordable, scalable solutions to create facilities that are more effectively used. To solve this problem, the Dutch public-private partnership initiative SuGeST (Smart Buildings, Smart Future) is establishing an open, standard-based digital backbone for commercial real estate. By leveraging a decentralized, federated data model and semantic middleware, SuGeST unifies highly diverse data sources, including Building Information Modeling (BIM), Building Management Systems (BMS), and time-series sensor data, while securely keeping all data at their original sources. Built on FAIR data principles and closely aligned with international ontologies, such as Brick, SAREF, and BOT, the project delivers practical data structuring guidelines alongside an independent data layer proof-of-concept. Integration is achieved using a system integration approach. The framework is validated across two smart living labs at the Technical Universities of Delft (The Green Village) and Eindhoven. By improving data access, the independent layer simplifies algorithm training, making it easier to deploy specific MPC hardware and software as a building's base control system based on its semantic parameters. The independent layer aims to demonstrate a 20-25% reduction in system implementation time alongside a 10–20% improvement in energy efficiency and indoor climate comfort. Ultimately, the project provides a definitive, actionable roadmap for real estate owners, installers, and software vendors to claim true data ownership at the source and accelerate the sustainable transformation of the built environment.

talks.title: From Ontology Design to Operationalised Interoperability: The Semantic Resource Interface (SRI)
talks.speaker: Henon Mengistu Lamboro, Cécile Rabrait, Jan Mayer and Dušan Gabrijelčič
talks.abstract: Semantic technologies are widely recognised as a means to achieve interoperability in heterogeneous digital ecosystems. However, many ontology-driven initiatives remain limited to conceptual modelling activities and fail to demonstrate how semantic models can be integrated into operational data exchange infrastructures. This work presents the Semantic Resource Interface (SRI), an interoperability component developed within the Horizon Europe RESONANCE project to enable semantic integration across buildings, energy management systems, electric vehicle charging infrastructure, IoT devices, and flexibility services. In industrial environments, these systems operate in isolated silos, having heterogeneous data models, APIs, naming conventions, and various interpretations of identical concepts, which makes semantic interoperability both challenging and costly. Beyond integration at the data level, a key challenge is enabling a continuous bridge between heterogeneous but non-homogenised data sources and downstream energy applications and services. To overcome this challenge at an operational level, we designed the RESONANCE ontology that contains five ontology modules that reuse existing standard energy domain ontologies like SAREF (The Smart Applications REFerence Ontology) and its extensions SAREF4ENER and SAREF4BLDG. Then we implemented a shared, common semantic interoperability component, the Semantic Resource Interface (SRI).

talks.title: Schiphol’s Linked Data Approach for Aviation Asset Information Exchange
talks.speaker: Ad Ruijl and Jakko Heinen
talks.abstract: Since 2019, Amsterdam Airport Schiphol has been building a semantic foundation for exchanging and managing asset information across systems, projects and contractors. Asset data is exchanged using IFC-XML messages and modelled with the Data Dictionary Schiphol (DDS), a linked-data ontology describing asset types, properties, documents, locations and definitions in a standardised way. The resulting RDF data is stored in Schiphol’s Central Data Facility, known as the CDV, which acts as a semantic source of truth for operational asset information.  This use case shows how semantic technology is applied in a complex aviation asset environment where reliable information is essential for design, handover, maintenance and decision-making. With the introduction of the Assetviewer in 2025, the CDV becomes visually accessible to end users. Users can explore assets, properties, locations, documents and definitions directly from the linked-data layer, making semantic models useful beyond system integration alone.  Together with Wistor, Schiphol is extending this foundation towards IFC model viewing, BIM exploration, project-specific information windows, ILS automation and contextual SHACL validation. A key next step is DDS 4.0, which separates conceptual meaning, physical data structures and validation logic more explicitly, drawing on principles from MIM and NEN 2660. This makes the model more compact, flexible and maintainable, while enabling stronger validation of project deliverables.  The presentation demonstrates how linked data, ontologies and SHACL can support practical asset information exchange in aviation, and how semantic technology can help verify whether projects have delivered the asset data that was agreed contractually and operationally.

title: (En-)Coding The Knowledge Graph Stack
label: Tutorial
description:
(En-)Coding The Knowledge Graph Stack: RDF, RDFS, SPARQL, SHACL, (YARR)RML

Knowledge Graphs help break down data silos by connecting heterogeneous sources into a shared, machine interpretable data layer. Too often, the stack driving this technology remains a mystery. This hands-on tutorial introduces the underlying technologies for building RDF-based knowledge graphs. In two sessions, participants will learn to understand and create graphs, apply ontologies, build constraints and ingest data. The first half of the tutorial, we will start with an introduction into triples, how they can be built with a simple text editor and how they already form a graph. Some of the terms carry a fixed semantics for building ontologies (RDFS, OWL) or are from already established vocabularies, and we will explore how to use them in a practical setting. Later that session, we explore SPARQL for extracting our newly created data. In the second half of the tutorial, we jump into ingestion and constraints. First, we create a data ingestion pipeline using YARRRML, a simpler subset of R2RML and RML, the standardized language for creating declarative pipelines. Later, we applied data quality checks with SHACL, ensuring that our graph data is structurally consistent, ensuring a high degree of data quality.

talks.title: Ontology-Aware Prompting for Knowledge Graph Construction from Text
talks.speaker: Balram Tiwari, Italo Oliveira, Asep Fajar Firmansyah, Hamada M Zahera, Frank Hopfgartner and Axel-Cyrille Ngonga Ngomo
talks.abstract: Constructing Knowledge Graphs (KGs) from unstructured text has traditionally relied on multi-stage pipelines combining Named Entity Recognition, Relation Extraction, and Entity Linking components. These architectures are costly to adapt to new domains and suffer from error propagation across stages. While Large Language Models (LLMs) enable end-to-end triple generation from text, their direct application introduces two key challenges: (1) hallucination, where generated facts are not supported by the input text, and (2) ontology misalignment, where extracted entities and relations violate the constraints of a target schema. To address these limitations, we propose an ontology-aware multi-prompt framework that integrates the target ontology into the prompting process and applies hierarchical verification after triple generation. Specifically, we combine Tree-of-Thoughts-style reasoning for structured exploration, schema-constrained OpenIE, and relaxed triple generation to produce a diverse set of candidate triples while maintaining ontological awareness. A rule-based three-filter filtering module then refines these candidates using cross-prompt agreement, evidence grounding, and surface-form alignment, without relying on external toolchains. Experiments on Text2KGBench, including DBpedia-WebNLG and Wikidata-TekGen, show improvements of up to 2.3 times over LLM-based baselines, together with hallucination rates below 0.20 in most domains and ontology conformance above 0.90 on most DBpedia-WebNLG domains. The framework is released as open-source and available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ontology-aware-kg-construction-2B0C.

talks.title: Best Practices in Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Systematic Evaluation
talks.speaker: Yan-Ying Liao, Diego Collarana, Christopher Ingo Pack, Alexander Graß, Andreas Both, Stefan Decker and Christian Beecks
talks.abstract: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) enhances Large Language Models (LLMs) by integrating knowledge graphs for structured retrieval and reasoning. However, the design space of GraphRAG systems is vast, and systematic guidance on optimal configurations remains scarce. In this paper, we present a comprehensive empirical study identifying best practices across the three core stages of the GraphRAG pipeline: graph-based indexing, graph-guided retrieval, and graph-enhanced generation. Through extensive experiments on multiple datasets (MSMARCO, HotpotQA, and a domain-specific legal corpus), we evaluate key design decisions, including chunking strategies, embedding model selection, prompt engineering for triplet extraction, entity resolution, retriever architectures, traversal depths, reranking models, and graph representation formats for LLM prompts. Our results show that hierarchical chunking at 512 tokens, schema-based extraction prompts, a combined Hypothetical Question and Entities retriever with cross-encoder reranking, and code-like graph representations (GraphML) yield robust performance across domains. We apply the identified best practices to a real-world use case within EU banking regulations, constructing a knowledge graph from the Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR) and the Capital Requirements Directive (CRD IV). A comparative evaluation demonstrates that the optimised GraphRAG system consistently outperforms Naive RAG, HyDE RAG, and Hybrid RAG, achieving overall win rates of 60.6%, 58.0%, and 67.4%, respectively, as judged by an LLM evaluator across comprehensiveness, diversity, empowerment, and correctness metrics. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for deploying GraphRAG in domain-specific, privacy-sensitive settings using open-source models.

talks.title: OntoExtend: A Framework for Requirement-driven and Scalable Ontology Extension with LLMs
talks.speaker: Anna Sofia Lippolis, Javad Saeedizade, Eva Blomqvist, Aldo Gangemi, Andrea Giovanni Nuzzolese, Robin Keskisärkkä, Stefan Schmid and Simon Blattner
talks.abstract: Ontology extension refers to the process of enriching an existing ontology in response to emerging requirements, making it more complete. This task is a resource-intensive and error-prone process. Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promising performance on generating ontologies from scratch, but current approaches rarely tie ontology extension explicitly to requirements or reusable core models, and offer limited, systematic evaluation of LLM outputs. This paper intro- duces OntoExtend, a requirements-driven framework for ontology extension with LLMs. It uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over relevant input ontologies and requirements in the form of competency questions to propose grounded extensions. To evaluate OntoExtend, we propose a multidimensional evaluation, including structural and functional assessment, as well as six ontology engineers who evaluate the generated extensions. The framework is instantiated and assessed on two use cases: a publicly available EU-project ontology and an industrial ontology. The results indicate little to no structural and logical issues and ontology engineers with high Fleiss inter-annotator agreement (Po) reported the generated fragments as semantically and syntactically correct, needing minor and moderate changes before being integrated into the input ontologies. These results suggest that the OntoExtend framework can support effective ontology extension in real-world scenarios.

talks.title: Surprising Effectiveness of Self-Demonstrations in Enhancing Schema-Ontology Mapping with LLMs
talks.speaker: Siddhesh Thombre, Manasi Patwardhan and Sunita Sarawagi
talks.abstract: Integrating heterogeneous relational databases into a centralized ontology remains a persistent challenge in enterprise knowledge representation, primarily due to semantic heterogeneity, cryptic schema naming, missing metadata, and the abstraction gap between relational schemas and ontological models. Although large language models (LLMs) offer strong semantic reasoning capabilities, we show that directly applying them through one-shot prompting or naïve multi-stage pipelines leads to poor performance for schema–ontology mapping. This paper presents a self-demonstration-driven approach that combines a neuro-symbolic task decomposition with a novel mechanism for automatically generating pattern-guided, dependency-aware demonstrations to address this integration challenge. Our approach incorporates two key strategies to achieve substantial accuracy gains over existing LLM-based schema integration methods: (i) a neuro-symbolic decomposition of the task into cascaded sub-tasks, where symbolic constraints structure the search space and LLMs perform semantic reasoning within each focused sub-task, and (ii) self-generated demonstrations guided by domain-agnostic patterns to supervise each sub-task. Experiments on three of the most challenging scenarios from the RODI benchmark show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, substantially outperforming (~25 percentage points F1 improvements) both traditional schema-to-ontology mapping techniques and recent LLM-based schema-to-ontology and schema matching approaches. Ablation studies further reveal the significant benefits of pattern-guided self-demonstrations and the complementary benefits of neuro-symbolic task decomposition.

talks.title: Building Enterprise Knowledge Graphs for an Agentic World [SP]
talks.speaker: Marcel Fröhlich (Eccenca)
talks.abstract: As enterprise AI shifts from conversational models to autonomous agentic workflows, the need for deterministic, verifiable, and dynamic grounding is critical. While semantic knowledge graphs provide the symbolic backbone necessary for trust, explainability, and enterprise governance, static repositories are insufficient for high-velocity agentic loops. To support autonomous systems, knowledge graphs must evolve into active semantic execution layers that treat knowledge graphs as modular, actionable components. Moving beyond standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), organizations must expose semantic layers as dynamic, governable toolsets. AI agents require standardized communication protocols (like MCP) to contextually discover and interact with role-specific knowledge domains. This enables agents not just to retrieve data, but to use encapsulated logic for complex, multi-step reasoning. Crucially, empowering agents to participate in data creation and modification demands strictly governed action spaces. By establishing guardrails through shape-constrained validation, repeatable rule blocks, tightly scoped execution parameters and mandatory human in the loop, systems can ensure that agent-driven modifications yield transparent, verified changes. Adopting these actionable patterns enable agents to safely reason over, interact with, and evolve complex data ecosystems.

talks.title: Comparing Knowledge Graph Use in Large Scale Technical Documentation Projects
talks.speaker: Martin Blumbach and Ulrike Parson
talks.abstract: Technical product documentation helps customers use the full potential of complex products. However, as release cycles shorten, variants grow and reliable data for agentic AI is required, technical documentation faces rising demands.  Knowledge graphs organize product information and connect data across enterprise silos, making them useful for technical documentation. They also offer more reliable ground truth for agentic AI than vector RAG-based document ingestion, which often has issues with multi-hop retrieval and inconsistent terminology.  From an enterprise architecture point of view, a knowledge graph platform sits like a “spider in the web” between data sources and content delivery.  We present and compare the use of knowledge graphs in different (non-joint) large-scale documentation projects. Both projects have knowledge graphs in productive use, and each project represents a difficult scenario for technical documentation: * Endress+Hauser (represented by parson): Smaller, built-to-order products for process automation with a very high number of product variants * Ericsson: Larger software products for 5G core networks with a common, highly configurable platform  The session will have the following structure: * Introduction to the projects  ** Why use knowledge graphs  ** Objectives of projects  ** Scope of the solutions * System architecture and current implementation status  ** Components  ** W3C standards vs. proprietary solutions  ** Semantic models for product structures and  information types  ** Automation of processes  ** Integration with genAI * Future use  ** Integration of chatbot for content delivery  ** Extension of documentation solution to corporate  semantic middleware and knowledge hub  ** MCP server integration  ** Use of AI agents  ** Generate smart content from legacy content * Learnings  ** How to manage the implementation project  ** How to convince stakeholders  ** Change management and changed ways of working; new  roles for technical communicators  ** How to build up knowledge in semantic modeling

talks.title: Knowledge Graphs and Agentic AI for Legacy System Comprehension
talks.speaker: Ali Khalili, Mahmood Shafeie Zargar and Peter Schaap
talks.abstract: Legacy mainframe systems support critical financial operations in many large institutions. However, their internal logic, spanning decades of COBOL programs, batch job chains, flat files, and data flows, is rarely documented in a form accessible to new employees. When key engineers leave, institutional knowledge leaves with them — and in regulated industries, that gap is also a compliance exposure: frameworks such as BCBS 239 require banks to understand and demonstrate how critical risk and reporting data flows end-to-end. This talk presents how DIM (Data Insights Monitor), an agentic AI platform developed at Deloitte, was applied at a large bank in the Netherlands to make its legacy batch processing system queryable by anyone and its lineage demonstrable to regulators. The structure of the legacy system — its jobs, procs, steps, programs, applications, data groups and data elements — was modeled as a knowledge graph. DIM sits on top of it, translating natural language questions into graph queries and returning answers as text, tables, or interactive lineage diagrams. A business analyst can ask “show me the data lineage path between these two jobs” or “which programs depend on this data item?” without writing a single line of code. Beyond query translation, the platform brings together two distinct bodies of knowledge — the system’s code, modeled as a knowledge graph, and its surrounding documentation (domain glossaries, operations notes, change records) — through two complementary retrieval modes: graph RAG over the structured lineage and vector RAG over the documentation corpus. A guide library encoding domain rules and terminology steers interpretation, and a self-learning pipeline captures successful patterns from each interaction and feeds them back for future use. A model routing layer selects the appropriate LLM tier per question — fast for lookups, reasoning for impact analysis — keeping cost proportional to task complexity. talks.title: ISGBot: An Agentic Multimodal Knowledge Framework for Semantic Access to the Interinstitutional Style Guide
talks.speaker: Giorgos Filandrianos, Vassilis Tzouvaras, Giorgos Stamou
talks.abstract: The Interinstitutional Style Guide (ISG) is the primary reference for drafting, editing, translating and publishing documents across the European Union institutions. While the guide contains a large body of editorial, linguistic, legal and publication knowledge, its size and complexity can make the retrieval of relevant information challenging, particularly for users unfamiliar with its structure. To address this challenge, we developed ISGBot, an agentic knowledge framework that combines multimodal retrieval, semantic technologies, reference data and Large Language Models to provide conversational access to the content of the ISG.  ISGBot integrates information from PDF documents, extracted text, tables, images, captions, metadata and structured semantic resources represented in RDF and SKOS. A multimodal semantic representation layer combines text embeddings, image embeddings and semantic relations, while concepts identified within the content are linked to authoritative reference data and controlled vocabularies from EU Vocabularies. The retrieval architecture combines BM25, dense vector retrieval using Sentence-Transformers and FAISS, cross-encoder reranking, and RDF/SKOS graph navigation.  Unlike traditional Retrieval-Augmented Generation approaches, ISGBot employs an agentic retrieval loop in which Large Language Models assess context sufficiency, reformulate queries, consolidate evidence and generate grounded responses. The prototype was developed and validated in close collaboration with the ISG team of the Publications Office of the European Union, whose feedback was used to evaluate and refine the system. The resulting framework demonstrates how multimodal retrieval, semantic technologies and agentic AI can be combined to provide evidence-based access to complex organisational knowledge resources.

talks.title: Explaining RGNN Predictions on Knowledge Graphs via LRP 🎖️
talks.speaker: Franz Krause and Heiko Paulheim
talks.abstract: Relational Graph Neural Networks (RGNNs) have become powerful tools for learning on relational graph structures such as RDF knowledge graphs (KGs), achieving state-of-the-art performance in tasks such as node classification and link prediction. However, their black-box nature conflicts with a central objective of KGs: enabling transparent and interpretable knowledge-based systems. As a result, predictions produced by RGNNs are often difficult to explain in terms of the graph structure itself. In this work, we present a generalized framework for explaining RGNN predictions using Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation (LRP). The approach traces predictions through the relational message-passing process and redistributes signed relevance scores to nodes, edges, and multi-hop paths. In doing so, it establishes a semantic predictive loop in which predictions derived from the KG structure can themselves be explained with respect to the underlying computation graph. Beyond extending relevance propagation to relational message passing, the framework unifies structure-oriented and embedding-oriented explanations by linking graph components to embedding-level contributions. Experiments on standard KG learning benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method yields faithful and interpretable explanations of RGNN predictions across multiple structural levels.

talks.title: A Semantic Framework for the Synthesis of Causal Knowledge 🎖️
talks.speaker: Katrin Ehrenmüller, Lucas Kook, Fajar J. Ekaputra and Marta Sabou
talks.abstract: MOTIVATION: AI systems relying solely on correlations often fail when training and production distributions differ, limiting their utility for reliable decision-making. While incorporating causal knowledge offers a more robust alternative, synthesizing such knowledge from heterogeneous sources remains a fragmented and cognitively demanding task. There is currently a lack of support for integrating, comparing, and resolving discrepancies between multiple, often conflicting, causal graphs.  OBJECTIVES: We present SoCK (Synthesis of Causal Knowledge), a semantic framework designed to integrate, analyse, and explore causal graphs derived from heterogeneous sources. Our goal is to provide a unified representation of causal knowledge that supports expert-in-the-loop exploration and transforms differing causal graphs into a queryable knowledge base. The framework aims to provide an accessible interface for multiple stakeholders, focusing on knowledge engineers, causal discovery researchers, and domain experts.  METHODS: Following a requirements-driven design, we developed three core contributions: (i) the SoCK ontology provides a unified formalization of causal graphs and their provenance; (ii) the Causal Knowledge Graph integrates multi-source inputs into a unified knowledge base; and (iii) an Exploration Interface operationalizes complex semantic queries through task-based interactions.  RESULTS: We evaluate SoCK using the CausalAssembly benchmark dataset. Results demonstrate that the ontology provides high representational coverage, successfully answering 14 out of 15 competency questions. Furthermore, scenario-based evaluations show that the framework effectively supports stakeholder tasks, such as algorithm selection and structural discrepancy analysis, by enabling systematic comparison and exploration of causal graphs through the interface.  CONCLUSION: SoCK addresses a critical challenge in causal discovery by providing the first semantic infrastructure for managing the heterogeneity and ambiguity inherent in multi-source causal discovery. By integrating fragmented causal knowledge and providing an interactive exploration interface to query complex metadata, the framework offers a systematic foundation for comparing causal models and resolving structural causal discrepancies.

talks.title: When Knowledge Graph Relationships Still Matter
talks.speaker: Alex Romanova
talks.abstract: Modern language models increasingly recover signals of relatedness from text alone. They can support related-item ranking, entity clustering, and recommendation-style workflows without a separately modeled graph. For the knowledge graph community, this creates a timely and practical question: when do explicit graph relationships still add value beyond what strong text embeddings already capture?  This paper approaches that question carefully. It does not treat knowledge graphs as globally replaceable. Many KG roles — including semantic integration, provenance, governance, validation, querying, and domain modeling — remain distinct from embedding-based retrieval. Instead, we focus on a narrower class of use cases where relationship value is representational: recommendation, discovery, similarity search, related-item ranking, and relation recovery. In these settings, the question becomes measurable: do explicit relationships add recoverable signal beyond node text?  We introduce a relation-dependent diagnostic framework for measuring this boundary. We call the underlying phenomenon language-model encroachment: the growing ability of text-based representations to approximate relational signal traditionally supplied by explicit graph structure. Using an OpenAlex-derived scientific KG case study, we repeat the diagnostic across relation types, dataset slices, publication years, and text encoders. In each setting, text-derived and graph-derived representations are evaluated on the same held-out relationship recovery task. The results show that the graph–text boundary is not fixed. Some relation types are largely recoverable from text for this task. Others retain distinctive graph-derived signal.  The contribution is a practical diagnostic for KG engineering: if a relationship type adds signal beyond text, it may justify graph-engineering effort; if it does not add measurable signal, a text-first system may be sufficient for that task. This does not mean a KG is unnecessary overall, because many KG roles remain justified independently of embedding performance.

talks.title: Prototype Implementation to improve LLMs with structured legal knowledge
talks.speaker: Christian Dirschl and Sven Krantz-Knutzen
talks.abstract: Wolters Kluwer is a global leader in information solutions, software and services for professionals, combining deep domain expertise with advanced technology. Current GenAI solutions driven by LLMs and RAG hit a quality ceiling when it comes to answering complex domain questions. We have built a prototype to augment these GenAI solutions in our domain with a legal knowledge layer that aims to break this ceiling. In order to achieve that, we have on the one hand built a concept for a knowledge operating system that provides the required knowledge artefacts. And we have developed on the other hand a prototype to apply these knowledge artefacts within the GenAI business lifecycle. Overall, the main industry question is still, which knowledge with what granularity and expressiveness is needed where in the process to address best the quality gap. Creating, maintaining and providing complex knowledge artefacts is still a challenging task. Therefore, any approach that clearly states what is needed lowers the acceptance barrier and frees the necessary investments from the business to have this information available in the end. Our knowledge artefacts are built on semantic web standards and vocabularies in order to ensure scalability and sustainability in the future and provide a proper basis for enabling interoperability with other artefacts and other domains that we are serving at Wolters Kluwer. We will show preliminary answers to these business critical questions. We also think that our findings are applicable beyond the legal domain.

title: (En-)Coding The Knowledge Graph Stack
label: Tutorial
description:
(En-)Coding The Knowledge Graph Stack: RDF, RDFS, SPARQL, SHACL, (YARR)RML

Knowledge Graphs help break down data silos by connecting heterogeneous sources into a shared, machine interpretable data layer. Too often, the stack driving this technology remains a mystery. This hands-on tutorial introduces the underlying technologies for building RDF-based knowledge graphs. In two sessions, participants will learn to understand and create graphs, apply ontologies, build constraints and ingest data. The first half of the tutorial, we will start with an introduction into triples, how they can be built with a simple text editor and how they already form a graph. Some of the terms carry a fixed semantics for building ontologies (RDFS, OWL) or are from already established vocabularies, and we will explore how to use them in a practical setting. Later that session, we explore SPARQL for extracting our newly created data. In the second half of the tutorial, we jump into ingestion and constraints. First, we create a data ingestion pipeline using YARRRML, a simpler subset of R2RML and RML, the standardized language for creating declarative pipelines. Later, we applied data quality checks with SHACL, ensuring that our graph data is structurally consistent, ensuring a high degree of data quality.

talks.title: Neurosymbolic AI and Human-Centered Explainability: from Neuron Activations to Explanations and Back
talks.speaker: Alessandra Mileo (Dublin City University)
talks.abstract:
Neuro-Symbolic AI is becoming a fast-growing area of research. However, there is still a lot of potential for leveraging neuro-symbolic approaches to address the need for explainability and confidence. These are key requirements when it comes to using neural models in computer vision and language processing to support human experts in high-stake decision making. In this talk I will set the scene with preliminaries on Explainability and Interpretability, and cover approaches for understanding deep representations via concept-neuron association, co-activations analysis and knowledge graphs, and their applicability in real-world scenarios.

I will also discuss recent advances in the design of a neurosymbolic cycle for Human-centered explainability by identifying the key elements I believe are needed to create a full cycle from neurons' activation to human-centered explanations and back to model adaptation. We will discuss opportunities offered by Neuro-Symbolic integration, and open challenges in the design of such a cycle.

title: Agentic AI: May the Knowledge Graph Be with You!
label: Agentic AI: May the Knowledge Graph Be with You!
description:
Agentic AI: May the Knowledge Graph Be with You!

Fishbowl

Scheduled: September 16, from 5 to 6pm, in room Kabinet

Agentic AI needs Knowledge Graphs and vice versa – Discussion of Pros & Cons

This session will bring together two first-class citizens in the future AI ecosystem: AI Agents and Knowledge Graphs (KG). Statistics and Semantics. Educated guesses and educated statements. Both need each other and both profit from each other. Or is this wishful thinking of the semantic web community? The AI community might argue that creating a statistically sound guessing system based on factual data is better than trusting random knowledge collected by some humans... Let’s discuss!

The open discussion takes place in a fishbowl format. In this format everyone is invited to join the “panel” - that is like a fishbowl, set-up in the center of the room. We expect experts from the audience to kick-off the discussion and continue along our common thread.

We will steer the discussion around clear benefits for both worlds with questions like:

  • ​How can Semantics help Agentic AI with its quality ceiling gap challenge?
  • How can semantic technologies, how can KG’s help to trust the results of Agent AI models?
  • How can KGs help to maintain ownership of knowledge?
  • How can Agentic AI help to build and maintain Knowledge Graphs fast and with limited (human) resources?
  • How could an integrated semantic agentic AI pipeline look like that leverages the capabilities of both technologies?

As a wrap-up we will summarize the results together, identifying some major opportunities and risks. The more concrete requirements, use cases and solution strategies we gather from the participating audience, the higher the impact will be for further discussions on the second day of SEMANTiCS conference and further on.
