talks.title: From GOFAI to NewFAI - From Good Old Fashioned AI to New Fashioned AI
talks.speaker: Deborah McGuinness (Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute)
talks.abstract: Artificial intelligence has evolved from foundations grounded in explicit knowledge representation, formal semantics, and symbolic reasoning to a new AI landscape increasingly influenced—and sometimes dominated—by large language models, agents, and rapidly evolving generative technologies. Drawing on my perspective as a longtime ontology and semantics researcher and professor, I will discuss approaches that aim to leverage the strengths of both worlds. I will present emerging hybrid architectures that integrate ontologies and semantic technologies with LLM-based pipelines, illustrating how these approaches are reshaping several of my current research projects. I will also explore how this transition is transforming AI education. In particular, I will describe a new model for readings courses in fast-moving fields that I developed and used in my course on knowledge-graph-powered hybrid AI. I will then discuss exploratory approaches to incorporating generative and agentic AI into my ontology engineering course, including the design and classroom integration of an agentic teaching assistant. This assistant is intended to support students while reinforcing—not replacing—the critical thinking, conceptual modeling, and semantic discipline required for effective ontology engineering. Together, these experiences offer a practical view of how researchers and educators can connect AI’s foundations to its rapidly unfolding future.

talks.title: SEOntology: A Domain Ontology for Semantic Modeling of Search Engine Optimization Workflows 🎖️
talks.speaker: Emilija Gjorgjevska, David Riccitelli, Milos Jovanovik and Andrea Volpini
talks.abstract: SEO workflows remain difficult to automate and integrate because they span heterogeneous tools while relying on loosely structured data models that provide limited machine-interpretable representations of content, actions, and performance signals. This fragmentation hinders interoperability and makes provenance tracking across SEO systems brittle. We present SEOntology, a Schema.org-aligned OWL 2 ontology that models SEO workflows as knowledge-graph structures to support structured querying and provenance-aware analysis. The ontology enables queries for content-quality inspection, entity-coverage analysis, and end-to-end tracing of analytical actions through their inputs, outputs, and generated signals. We assess SEOntology via structural ontology evaluation and competency-question validation, and report supporting evidence from production deployment. These results indicate logical consistency, coverage of the defined requirements, and practical utility as a semantic integration layer for representing and querying SEO workflows. SEOntology is designed as a reusable semantic resource for knowledge-graph–driven and agent-assisted SEO systems, and is extensible toward emerging generative and AI-mediated search environments.

talks.title: Using gUFO patterns to create ontologies: unraveling the nature of employment contracts
talks.speaker: Kees Nieuwstad and Han Joosten
talks.abstract: The Dutch Police need a set of integrated domain ontologies to support their operations and information management. To achieve this goal, they initially adopted DOLCE (implemented in OWL) as an upper ontology to ground domain ontology development. However, DOLCE did not offer modeling patterns to ensure consistency and communication among modelers and stakeholders. The team ended up having different conventions and design decisions that harmed the goal achievement.  To overcome these challenges, the police team with our team joined forces to adopt gUFO as the backbone of the ontology development for this project. gUFO is a lightweight OWL implementation of the Unified Foundational Ontology (UFO) that consists of several ontology design patterns that solve common modeling problems in ontology engineering. When our teams worked with these patterns, we noticed that we obtained better communication and higher-quality models.  To streamline the application of gUFO patterns, we use OWL reasoning and implemented SPARQL queries that automatically validate ontology design choices continuously for all developers involved in the process. Therefore, we created a collaborative environment that ensures certain ontology quality metrics, following gUFO patterns. One of these patterns allows us to represent different types of employment contracts faithfully. For example, in gUFO, a relator is a relationship treated as a thing in its own right. Instead of just saying "John works for the Police", "John’s contract" is created as a concrete entity that can have its own properties like a start date or legal obligations. In this case, the relator connects an employee to the Police organization. We do not only adopt the pattern but also enforce it via an automated validation pipeline, quickly detecting errors.

talks.title: AI-Driven Ontology Development for Multi-Lingual and Multi-Jurisdiction Financial Services - the HYPOPASS case
talks.speaker: Leon Roseleur
talks.abstract: Creating a data standard across multiple jurisdictions isn't a technology problem. The real challenge lays in the fact that the same concept often has a different meaning depending on the legal system, language, or sector in which it is used. Standardizing on the technical layer does not solve those differences, unless organizations connect on both the semantic, the legal and the process-level. Otherwise, interoperability remains limited. We refer to this challenge as the legal-semantic gap. A good example is HypoPass, a Belgian-Dutch mortgage industry initiative that connects 16 banks and thousands of financial advisors across Belgium. The initiative spans three languages (Dutch, French and English), brings together 14 different data models and handles different jurisdictions across Wallonia, Flanders and Brussels. We were asked to develop interoperability between all parties involved. The complete data exchange consisted of approximately 4,800 definitions. Using conventional methods, this exercise was expected to take around 18 months. By applying an AI-supported methodology aligned with the European Interoperability Framework (EIF), we delivered a validated ontology within 13 weeks while maintaining an error rate below 0.5% - connecting the legal, semantic, organizational and layer. A key design principle is that experts remain in control throughout the process. AI performs the initial analysis and proposes mappings, while legal, business and domain specialists validate the results before moving to the next stage. This approach reduces the effort required per concept from hours to minutes and shortens overall delivery timelines tremendously. After this initial project, the same method tested and applied within various use cases spanning from Tax Office, Customs, Life Sciences and company law.

talks.title: Synthology: Ontology-Based Data Generation for Neurosymbolic Reasoning
talks.speaker: Vincent Van Schependom, Cas Proost and Pieter Bonte
talks.abstract: Symbolic reasoners offer a simple contract: provide an ontology, receive entailments. Neurosymbolic reasoners promise the same task with added scalability and tolerance to noise, but break this contract by requiring an ontology-specific training dataset, which in most cases does not exist and must be gathered from scratch. This bottleneck blocks practitioners from applying neurosymbolic reasoners to new ontologies. We present Synthology, an ontology-agnostic synthetic data generator that closes this gap by producing the required training data from any OWL 2 RL ontology, with no need for manual data gathering. Synthology engineers data through ontology-guided backward-chaining proof search, which guarantees deep multi-hop derivations by construction, and introduces proof-based negative sampling. Together, these properties force models to traverse the full reasoning chain to correctly classify triples.  Our evaluation shows that a model trained on Synthology  data outperforms models trained on baseline data, with  a particularly robust advantage in rejecting near-miss  negatives. Proof-based negative sampling yields  consistent gains over random and constrained sampling  on all learning-quality metrics, and Synthology scales  to ontologies on which traditional (ontology specific)  generators run out of memory. To our knowledge,  Synthology is the first ontology-agnostic synthetic  data generator that provides multi-hop coverage,  near-miss negatives, and derivation metadata by  construction, a step toward making neurosymbolic  reasoners as readily deployable on a new ontology as  their symbolic counterparts.

talks.title: Privacy-Preserving Sharing of Knowledge Graphs at the Bank of Italy
talks.speaker: Luigi Bellomarini, Costanza Catalano, Andrea Coletta and Michela Iezzi
talks.abstract: Corporate ownership graphs are a strategic knowledge asset for banking supervision and financial intelligence, but their dissemination is constrained by strict confidentiality requirements. This talk presents an industrial case study from the Central Bank of Italy on privacy-preserving sharing of corporate ownership Knowledge Graphs (KGs). In our setting, the KG is not only an extensional graph of asserted ownership triples, but a semantic knowledge base whose intensional layer is specified by Datalog rules. These rules define entailment over the graph and derive supervisory notions such as corporate control, ultimate control, joint control, integrated ownership, and qualifying holdings. As a result, what must be protected is not only the explicit graph, but the combination of asserted data and rule-based inferences.  This requirement is central in institutional data-sharing  scenarios involving external analysts, researchers, and  supervisory partners. Existing anonymization and  graph-sanitization techniques typically focus on  structural disclosure in the released graph, while they do  not address confidential information that may be  reconstructed through the semantic rule layer. This gap is  relevant as KGs become core assets for analytics and  grounding layers for LLM-based applications in  high-confidentiality domains. We introduce a semantic anonymization framework for corporate ownership KGs. The method transforms the graph through controlled node and edge additions, entity relabeling, and weight perturbation, while taking the Datalog program into account to prevent both direct disclosure and inference-based leakage. We validate the framework on the Central Bank of Italy ownership dataset and on external benchmarks, assessing formal privacy protection, preservation of supervisory entailments, structural distortion, and downstream analytical utility. The experiments show that the anonymized KGs retain the semantic content required for regulatory analysis while preventing the disclosure of confidential information.

talks.title: From Linked Data to AI-Ready Data: Five Floors, and How to Build Them [SP]
talks.speaker: Agis Papantoniou (Cognizone)
talks.abstract: Every organisation now says it wants its data to be "AI-ready". Almost nobody can say what that means, or how to get there - and the usual answer, put the documents in a vector database and connect an LLM, produces impressive demos that stall before production. The model is rarely the problem. The data underneath it is.This talk introduces a practical framework for AI-ready data: five floors, built foundation-first, in the spirit of Tim Berners-Lee's five-star model for linked open data. Each floor is a state your data is either in or not, testable by specific conditions that can be checked in a pragmatic way.Most of the session focuses on how the floors get built. For every new floor we discuss what it provides, how to tell whether you have successfully built it, and what it takes to reach the next one.This is based on a decade of experience building production knowledge graphs for EU institutions and regulated industries.

talks.title: Automated legal reasoning system for generating draft responses to claims, based on Neurosymbolic AI on knowledge graphs.
talks.speaker: Ricardo Alonso-Maturana, Angel Esteban Moreno-Beltrán, Marcos Campazas, Susana López-Sola and Karmele Alonso Aia
talks.abstract: If this case is selected, the final case presentation is subject to approval by our client. An insurance entity manages thousands of lawsuits annually across two highly complex regulatory domains: extraordinary risks (floods, earthquakes, terrorist attacks) and compulsory motor vehicle insurance. Each case file arrives as heterogeneous documentary chaos: procedural briefs, expert reports, photographs, scanned administrative files. Processing it through traditional methods represents weeks of specialized legal work, with the risk of argumentative inconsistency and exposure to deadlines that the judicial system does not forgive. GNOSS has built and deployed an automated legal reasoning system that does not merely retrieve relevant documents, but reasons over them. Its core is a knowledge graph encoding the regulatory pyramid applicable to the fund — from the Constitution and EU law down to administrative circulars — integrated with a jurisprudential layer of five thousand CENDOJ rulings. The system extracts the legally material entities from the case file, classifies the case, traverses the corresponding argumentative chain, and identifies the optimal procedural strategy from twelve predefined options. Each inference is an examinable logical instance, not a statistical prediction. The result is a tool that complies by design with the explainability and auditability requirements that the European AI Act demands of high-risk systems. The lawyer does not receive an answer: they receive a line of reasoning they can follow, challenge, and sign. What previously required days of work is completed in minutes, with full traceability and systematic argumentative consistency.

talks.title: Creating an AI-ready fundament for the Dutch Digital System for the Environment and Planning Act
talks.speaker: Jan Lyckle Bijlsma and Art Ligthart
talks.abstract: AI applications for the Dutch Digital System for the Environment and Planning Act (DSO: Digitaal Stelsel Omgevingswet) increasingly support citizens and professionals in interpreting environmental and planning regulations. However, these applications operate in a legally sensitive domain in which answer quality must not only be useful, but also correct, traceable, and explainable. This creates a need for a semantic infrastructure that can bridge user language and legal concepts, connect the concepts between different domains and create a fundament for AI applications to build on. Our work combines semantic modelling of DSO data with graph-based modelling of legal texts from national, provincial, municipal, and water authority sources. The graph links user-facing activities, legal activities, legal rules, concepts, and legislative structure. To support legal traceability, statutes and decrees were transformed from XML into RDF graph structures using a dedicated ontology in combination with the ontology of European Legislation Identifier (ELI). A graph agent then decomposes a user question into key terms and user-facing activities. The agent then traverses through the graph to retrieve relevant legal context, and re-ranks candidate documents. This approach allows the modelling of knowledge graphs to be directly used as input for (LLM-based) AI-solutions, resulting in a clearer overview of used sources and provides visualisation potential for increased trust and understanding from the user’s perspective.

talks.title: Engineering the Enterprise Semantic Layer: From Business Meaning to Machine-Executable Data Architecture [SP]
talks.speaker: Thomas Kaminski (DigitalScience)
talks.abstract: Business language and technical data architecture still live in separate worlds and that gap is quietly undermining enterprise AI initiatives. Data catalogs and APIs have improved access to data, but they rarely capture what that data means or how it connects to the business concepts that govern it.This session presents a concise engineering blueprint for an Enterprise Semantic Layer: an architectural approach that connects Business Object ontologies, physical data assets, and technical metadata through explicit semantic models and schema mappings. Drawing on real enterprise implementations, Thomas Kaminski (Senior Knowledge Graph Solutions Engineer, Digital Science / metaphacts) shows how RDF-based schema representations and business object modeling give both humans and AI agents a shared, machine-interpretable view of the enterprise data landscape.In 15 minutes, you'll walk away understanding how this framework transforms Enterprise Information Architecture from static documentation into an operational layer that enables semantic data discovery, automated lineage and explainable AI at enterprise scale.

talks.title: A Knowledge Graph–Based Framework for Harmonising and Comparing Social Surveys 🎖️
talks.speaker: Sara Zuppiroli, Silvia Cappa and Andrea Giovanni Nuzzolese
talks.abstract: A wide range of tools in the social sciences, stemming from numerous studies in economics, political science, and sociology, requires systematic methods for reuse, integration, and international comparison. To address this challenge, we present an integrated software archi- tecture that combines ontological modelling and knowledge-extraction techniques to detect, import, and reuse questionnaires in a simple and intuitive way. The system integrates a user-friendly web interface, a ques- tionnaire import module, and a semantic knowledge graph that formalizes and interlinks core survey entities—such as questions, variables, and groups. This infrastructure supports both the construction of new questionnaires and meaningful comparison across heterogeneous studies and diverse contexts. Built upon semantic technologies and established ontology design patterns, the architecture ensures an interoperable representation of survey components and their relationships to social variables. Overall, the proposed system addresses a critical limitation of current research infrastructures in the social sciences: the difficulty of designing FAIR-by-design survey instruments capable of identifying, operationalis- ing, and systematically comparing relevant social variables across coun- tries and over time.

talks.title: From File Systems to Knowledge Graphs: A Multi-Phase Workflow for the Description of Born-Digital Personal Archives 🎖️
talks.speaker: Lucia Giagnolini and Paolo Bonora
talks.abstract: Background: Born-digital personal archives present novel descriptive challenges that conventional archival methods are not equipped to address. Their scale, format heterogeneity, and multi-layered stratification — physical, logical, and conceptual — require a representational framework capable of capturing document structure, provenance, integrity, and relational contexts. The increasing vol- ume of born-digital archives received by cultural heritage institutions makes the development of automated and scalable description methodologies an urgent prac- tical priority. Methods: This paper presents a replicable five-phase pipeline, grounded in the Born-Digital Ontology (BoDi) — a formal extension of Records in Contexts Ontology (RiC-O) integrating PREMIS, PROV-O, and LRMoo — that transforms born- digital personal archive directories into RDF knowledge bases. The phases are: (1) file system ingestion, comprising SHA-256 integrity verification, parallel multi- tool metadata extraction, and triplestore loading; (2) SPARQL-based validation and rule-based enrichment, including cross-tool metadata alignment, document classi- fication, and duplicate detection; (3) hybrid enrichment combining expert biblio- graphic curation with automated LLM-based description generation; (4) chain-of- custody reconstruction; and (5) selective entity-level redaction for privacy-aware dissemination. Results: Evaluated on the Valerio Evangelisti Archive — 78,211 files and 11,135 folders totaling 2.1 TB across three storage media — the pipeline generated 61,154,322 RDF triples across 13 named graphs with minimal manual interven- tion. The resulting knowledge base supports querying across structural, typological, temporal, and relational dimensions, enabling analyses — from duplicate detection across storage media to correlation of archival activity with editorial output — that conventional finding aids cannot support. Conclusions: Born-digital archives present a double challenge: their fragility raises preservation concerns, while their scale renders manual description effectively impossible. The pipeline addresses both by inverting the framing: the properties that make born-digital materials resistant to conventional methods become, within a formal framework, sources of descriptive richness without equivalent in the analog domain. Ontological modeling combined with automated processing and human-in-the-loop validation offers a viable and empirically demonstrated path toward semantic description of born-digital cultural heritage at scale.

talks.title: From MARC21 to WEMI Without a Library-Software Vendor: A Semantic-Platform Bet
talks.speaker: Jeroen Wouters
talks.abstract: Cultuurconnect runs the central catalogue that 300 Flemish public libraries use to catalogue their holdings, with around 60 cataloguers working in it on a typical day. The data sits in MARC21, the legacy library exchange format, even though IFLA's WEMI/LRM model has been the agreed direction for years and most library-software vendors are still slow to ship against it. In 2024 Cultuurconnect concluded that waiting for the next vendor release was not going to get them where they needed to be, and looked across the office floor in Ghent, where Inuits had been building a generic semantic platform called Elody. A joint proof of concept that summer turned into a full build a year later; the new system goes into production in June 2026.   Our pitch was contrarian: do not look for a library-software vendor that has yet to ship WEMI; pair a semantic-platform team with the customer's own domain expertise. The catalogue is now an entity-relation model with a thin collection service that distributes data to and from external sources (VIAF, Boekenbank, Muziekweb), with a real-time MARC21 stream kept alive for downstream consumers. The model holds roughly 3 million WEMI entities, is already published as Linked Open Data, and is shaped by cataloguers through ongoing sprint feedback — without compromising the WEMI model we were aiming for. The lesson we did not expect when we started: sector expertise is not the limiting factor in this kind of project. A serious technology partner paired with the customer's own domain people consistently beats a sector-specific software vendor that hasn't yet implemented the new standard.

talks.title: From confusion to confidence: why semantic data management matters now [SP]
talks.speaker: Ingrid Thurlings (SopraSteria)
talks.abstract: Trust in data is a strategic requirement: organisations cannot scale AI, satisfy regulations, or make confident decisions if they lack a shared, explicit understanding of what their data means. Today, that meaning is scattered across systems, documents and experts’ heads, making information hard to combine, interpret and reuse. This makes turning compliance with complex regulation, such as the EU AI Act, into a slow, fragile exercise.Semantic Data Management addresses this gap by making business concepts, relationships and rules explicit, shareable and machine‑readable. By grounding data in semantic models and knowledge graphs that are based on standards, organisations ensure that people and AI reason over the same reality. This “trust by design” approach creates an explainable data foundation, improves data quality, enables cross‑domain collaboration and unlocks advanced analytics and AI at scale.In highly regulated, multi‑stakeholder environments, the same principles transform legal and regulatory knowledge from static text into a living, operational asset. Knowledge graphs capture human legal interpretation in structured form, so compliance questions can be answered instantly and requirements translated into executable policies. For executives, the message is simple: semantics and knowledge graphs provide the missing strategic layer that connects data, AI and regulation into one trustworthy ecosystem.Join us if you want to know more about how a semantic backbone for your data can turn today’s regulatory and AI challenges into a coherent, trustworthy advantage for your entire organisation.

talks.title: DQV4AI: Representing AI Quality Dimensions for ISO and EU AI Act using the Data Quality Vocabulary
talks.speaker: Delaram Golpayegani, Beyza Yaman, Fabian Linde, Riccardo Albertoni and Harshvardhan J. Pandit
talks.abstract: As the use of AI proliferates rapidly, its development and deployment across all stages requires understanding and documentation regarding aspects such as its accuracy, fairness, and transparency---collectively called 'quality characteristics'. This has led to standardisation at forums such as ISO, and creation of obligations within regulations such as the EU's AI Act. To support this developing landscape, we assess the sufficiency of the Data Quality Vocabulary (DQV), which is a W3C Working Note, for representing AI quality dimensions. We find that while the DQV can be useful, some concepts require changes to the definition to enable use beyond datasets, for AI models and systems. Based on our findings, we propose updates to DQV concepts to allow a more general quality representation and provide taxonomies based on ISO/IEC DIS 25059 standard on AI quality models and the EU AI Act to represent key AI quality dimensions and examples of their use. We conclude with a discussion on the future of AI quality documentation, the role of Semantic Web standards, and facilitating interoperability across value chains and data spaces.

talks.title: SHACL, The Enabler For Human-Supported, LLM-Based Extraction With High Quality In The Engineering Legal Domain
talks.speaker: Achim Reiz, Gregor Seifer, Heinrich Terborg, Claudia Rachadell and León Martinez
talks.abstract: In the energy market, legally binding contracts between constructors and operators of a power plant define expectations regarding how a given plant should perform. If these guarantees are not met, the disadvantaged party can claim damages, the calculation of which is also specified within the contract document. Today, these contract documents consist mostly of unstructured text. As a result, calculating potential damages is labor-intensive. With graphs, we aim to transform these contracts into machine-readable documents and perform such checks automatically. Extracting the information with the correct set of terms is challenging: on the one hand, the diverse prose of legal texts requires LLM-based background knowledge for proper interpretation, as the documents do not follow strict guidelines regarding their content and structure. On the other hand, LLMs tend to hallucinate when dealing with vague or underspecified requirements. In the presented use case, we demonstrate how we utilize the Shape Constraint Language (SHACL) to build self-repairing LLM extraction pipelines for generating graphs from unstructured documents and enabling automatic data validation. While the ontology provides the context for what to extract, an integrated validation engine performs checks and delivers targeted repair messages to the LLM whenever the data does not conform to the desired constraints. That allows for a self-repairing data pipeline. Subsequently, we use a SHACL-defined UI to create a data interface for reviewing and editing accessible to legal scholars for a human in the loop architecture. talks.title: Populating and Evaluating a Knowledge Graph for Risk Management in Medical Devices
talks.speaker: Guilherme Semedo, Rodrigo Carvalho, Emanuel Valpaços, Liliana Teles, Mariana Pinto, Edmundo Miranda, Pedro Oliveira, Pedro Colarejo and Bruno Gago
talks.abstract: Manufacturers of medical devices are required to systematically manage risks under ISO 14971, a process that remains largely manual and dependent on domain expertise. Large Language Models offer interesting automation potential, but their adoption in regulated contexts requires traceable outputs, which is something that isolated LLM pipelines do not guarantee. This use case describes a methodology for grounding LLM risk management in a Knowledge Graph populated from real-world incident data, and introduces a consensus-based framework for evaluating the quality of the AI pipeline before deployment. We collected incident reports from the FDA MAUDE database across 26 product codes, yielding approximately 28,000 reports. A deduplication and normalization pipeline combining narrative normalization, text embeddings, and clustering reduced the results to a representative set of incidents per product family. For each incident cluster, we generated reasonably foreseeable sequences of events drawing on normalized narratives, patient problem codes, and device characteristics extracted from regulatory submission documents. Regulatory affairs specialists curated the outputs. Because no single ground-truth risk matrix exists under ISO 14971, we developed a structured expert consensus methodology. Panelists assessed baseline risk matrices, then reconciled them. Their agreed outputs form a gold standard against which further AI-generated risk matrices are benchmarked using a composite score. The methodology is replicable, device-agnostic, and designed to be integrated into electronic Quality Management Systems. Each ingestion cycle strengthens the Knowledge Graph, improving the quality of subsequent generation. To our knowledge, no published approach covers automated ISO 14971 compliant risk matrix generation with this combination of incident grounding, human curation, and continuous quality benchmarking.

talks.title: Semantic Annotation of Vaccination and Medication Information for Cross-Border Healthcare
talks.speaker: Filip Pattyn
talks.abstract: Healthcare information such as medications and vaccinations is typically recorded using national product names, local terminologies, and language-specific descriptions. While this information is meaningful within a country, it often becomes difficult to interpret across borders. Citizens travelling abroad and healthcare professionals treating international patients may struggle to identify equivalent medications, understand vaccination histories, or communicate treatment information effectively. This presentation introduces a semantic approach developed by FAQIR Institute to improve the cross-border understanding and exchange of medication and vaccination information. The approach uses internationally recognized standards and ontologies, including SNOMED CT, IDMP, the IDMP Ontology (IDMP-O), the ATC Classification System, and EMA SPOR controlled vocabularies. Vaccinations are linked to SNOMED CT concepts to identify vaccine types independently of national product names, while medications are represented through their active substances, pharmaceutical forms, strengths, and regulatory characteristics. FAQIR Institute maintains semantic representations of medicinal products from multiple countries. By combining semantic annotations with international classifications, the platform can identify equivalent or closely matching medicinal products and vaccine types across countries and languages. The hierarchical structures of SNOMED CT and ATC also enable semantic browsing, allowing users to discover broader or related therapeutic and vaccine categories. The use case demonstrates how semantic technologies can support cross-border healthcare, improve patient safety, enable language-independent understanding, and promote interoperability through the reuse of internationally recognized standards. The work is currently being integrated into the Personal Health Record Ontology (PHR-O) and implemented in Qwenda, a mobile application based on person-centric data vaults. Together, these initiatives illustrate how semantic technologies can transform national health information into interoperable, multilingual, and reusable knowledge that supports future digital health services.

talks.title: Start with the User, Arrive at the Ontology. Six Production Deployments, and the Road Back to RDF [SP]
talks.speaker: Jeroen Wouters (Inuits)
talks.abstract:
We were not semantic-data experts. That is not an apology; it is the reason this platform exists.

In the early 2010s we built the City of Antwerp's heritage DAMS on Drupal — common practice then, when stretching a CMS was the pragmatic shortcut for cultural-sector projects. By 2020 the cracks were visible: millions of assets, multiplied integrations, and a record-centric core holding back exactly the features users were asking for. A European research project with several Ghent museums gave us the rarest thing in this sector: permission to rebuild it the way we would build it today.

We did the thing you are not supposed to do at a semantics conference: we did not start from the ontology. The model was expressed in GraphQL and shaped by what cataloguers actually need to see. Our first version modelled the full LDES traversal in the schema and promptly hit the classic n+1 problem — and the fix became the product: each entity declares its own metadata interface and its own way of being fetched, from a REST call down to papers in someone's drawer, with a thin collection service stitching the rest together.

That backbone now runs six deployments with nothing in common: Antwerp's heritage collection, a police sensor network, a marine-science archive where a communications officer tags species from an ontology without ever seeing it, Flanders' central library catalogue, a performing-arts platform, and a corpus of ancient inscriptions at AlUla. LDES in; JSON-LD and IIIF out; open source throughout.

This talk closes where the journey arrives: a proof of concept in which the model is defined in RDF and everything else — including the GraphQL contract — is derived. Start with the user, and you arrive at the ontology through the other door. Afterwards, come and draw your collection at our booth.

talks.title: Decentralized Autonomous Grids: Neuro-Symbolic AI, W3C Semantic Web Standards, and Federated Knowledge Graphs in Virtualized Edge Networks
talks.speaker: Adrian Gjergjizi, Antun Ivan Kraljević and Diana Agejev
talks.abstract: Modern electrical grids are evolving rapidly, driven by the shift to clean energy and the surge of new, dynamic energy sources known as distributed energy resources (DERs). In the past, grid intelligence relied on centralized Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems. To build a more resilient grid, we are seeing a shift toward decentralized edge intelligence—separating the software that runs the grid from the older, fixed hardware it originally depended on. This presentation explores how electricity providers can move towards modern smart grids by using flexible software and universal data standards. We introduce a new framework, tested through the "Project Lyra" initiative, that places smart decision-making tools directly onto local substation computers. By using these specialized AI tools and standardized digital maps, local grid equipment can understand and manage energy data independently and safely as intended by the smart grid initiative. A highlight of this approach is 'Stochastic GraphRAG,' a neuro-symbolic reasoning framework that helps address physical telemetry uncertainty—cases where data is missing or unclear. By using native SPARQL 1.1 Monte Carlo simulations to analyze probability-weighted Named Graphs, edge agents can intelligently estimate the grid’s real-time status even with incomplete information. This allows equipment to coordinate independently and perform critical tasks like FLISR (automated fault location, isolation, and service restoration) using standard IEC 61850 messaging. Participants will gain practical insights on how to use containerized semantic architectures at the grid edge. You will learn practical ways to fix vendor-specific data heterogeneity by using ontologies to create a common language. Finally, we will show how to run probabilistic reasoning so that even resource-constrained industrial computers can make smart, reliable decisions on their own.

talks.title: From Sequential Language to Structural Intelligence: Toward Relationship-Aware AI
talks.speaker: Alex Romanova
talks.abstract: Large language models have transformed artificial intelligence by showing how much can be learned from language at scale. Their success has made language appear to be the dominant substrate of intelligence. This Blue Sky paper argues that this view is incomplete. We focus on one specific gap: what may be missing when relationships and structure are learned primarily through language.  We argue that LLMs face two language bottlenecks. First, they are token-sequence systems: even with attention and rich internal representations, they process and generate language through sequences of tokens. Second, their training data is human language, which is the sequential expression of cognition rather than the full relational process from which cognition emerges. Neuroscience gives reason to take this distinction seriously: the connectome and network neuroscience describe the brain in terms of elements, connections, and graph-like organization, while recent work argues that language is primarily a tool for communication rather than thought itself.  This suggests that LLMs learn from linguistic traces of intelligence, but not necessarily from the full relational processes that produce those traces. We therefore argue for relationship-aware AI as an open research direction: not a solved architecture, but a search for ways to combine linguistic fluency with explicit awareness of relationships and structure. The central distinction is between inference-time use of relationships and training-time learning from relationships. Many current systems add structure after a language model has already been trained, through retrieval, graph augmentation, tools, memory, or verification layers. These approaches are important, but the deeper Blue Sky challenge is to make relationships part of representation learning itself, so that structural awareness is learned by the model rather than supplied only after training.

talks.title: From Fact to Feeling: Narrative Knowledge Graphs for Human-AI Interaction
talks.speaker: Anna Sofia Lippolis and Luiz Do Valle Miranda
talks.abstract: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) and Large Language Models (LLMs) each capture a different dimension of human knowledge, and neither captures both. KGs excel at representing factual, structured information, yet remain blind to the perspectival and narrative texture through which humans construct and communicate meaning. LLMs absorb this texture implicitly from language, yet do so without explicit semantic structure, leaving their interpretive operations opaque, difficult to revise, and impossible to hold accountable. The next major challenge for Semantic Web research is developing formal infrastructures for the knowledge that falls between these two: perspectival, narrative, and metaphorically organized. We propose Narrative Knowledge Graphs (NKGs) as such an infrastructure. Grounded in computational hermeneutics, NKGs extend standard RDF foundations along three axes: perspective-annotated named graphs anchoring assertions to situated standpoints; narrative ontologies representing how the same events yield different accounts from different positions; and metaphorical frames, grounded in frame semantics, making explicit which conceptual structure a community or individual projects onto a domain. Together, these axes define a semantic layer designed to mediate between human experience and LLM-generated meaning. We position NKGs as a new fundamental layer for human-AI interaction, aimed at making machine-supported interpretation more explicit, revisable, and faithful to human meaning-making.

talks.title: Can a Knowledge Graph Fall Down? Embodied Knowledge Graphs for Humanoid Robots
talks.speaker: Blerina Spahiu and Loris Roveda
talks.abstract: Knowledge graphs (KGs) have become powerful instruments for representing, integrating, and querying knowledge. Humanoid robots expose a fundamental limitation of current world models: they can predict future states, but they rarely make explicit the semantic commitments needed to decide whether an object is reachable, a surface is supportive, a human is too close, or an action is unsafe. This paper argues that the next long-term challenge for Semantic Web and Knowledge Graph research is to build \emph{Embodied Knowledge Graphs}: dynamic, multimodal, uncertainty-aware semantic world models whose statements are grounded in geometry, perception, proprioception, affordances, physical constraints, and predicted action consequences. Such graphs would not merely answer ``what is true?'' but also make explicit which commitments are grounded enough to act upon, which remain risky, and which require further perception. This is not a proposal for adding a knowledge graph to a robot; it is a proposal for redefining what a knowledge graph must be when its statements can trigger physical action. Using humanoid semantic world reconstruction as a motivating stress test, the paper outlines a research agenda around joint geometric-semantic reconstruction, structural abstraction, affordance transfer, provenance, and self-maintenance. The proposal is intentionally high-risk: it asks whether knowledge graphs must become useful not only by representing the world, but by making embodied action safer, more recoverable, and more auditable than systems based only on latent world models or scene graphs.

Cool Solutions Meet Tricky Problems

A marketplace of ideas and challenges

Are you aware that there is a format during SEMANTiCS Conference that allows you to jump in and discuss spontaneously with fellow experts both from industry and academia about a pressing problem you are facing, or, about the real world relevance of a solution you have worked on for so long already?

Come and join our interactive session “Cool Solutions Meet Tricky Problems”.

This networking event follows a mini bar camp approach with a series of discussions in parallel break-out groups. Everybody joining is invited to bring his or her problem/approach to the table so that the break-out group may work on it collaboratively.

In these break-out dialogues you may contribute a pressing problem and ask for solution ideas. Or, you could sketch or demo your innovative idea and evaluate its relevance and usability.

talks.title: How good are Large Language Models at Ontology Engineering?
talks.speaker: Daniel Garijo (Universidad Politécnica de Madrid)
talks.abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized research across many domains, including knowledge engineering.

However, ontology development remains a complex and labor-intensive task that requires substantial domain expertise to ensure adequate competency question coverage, adherence to modeling best practices, effective vocabulary reuse, and high-quality documentation.

In this talk, I will present an overview of our recent work on using LLMs and agentic AI to support ontology engineering, with a particular focus on the end-to-end generation of ontologies from a set of competency questions. We explore how LLM-based agents can leverage external tools to iteratively design, validate, refine, and document ontologies rather than simply generating them in a single pass.

The talk will discuss the practical challenges of evaluating ontology quality, challenges of generating reliable benchmarks, as well as the importance of explainability, transparency, and traceability in the resulting ontologies. Overall, the talk will reflect on both the opportunities and limitations of LLMs in ontology engineering, and ask a broader question: should LLMs merely assist ontology engineers, or can they reliably take on a more autonomous role in the ontology engineering process?
